name: Danazol
lead: Danazol is an oral synthetic steroid derived from ethisterone, a testosterone relative. It has weak androgenic and anabolic activity together with antigonadotropic, progestogenic and functional anti-oestrogenic effects. It is a prescription drug used mainly for endometriosis, with approved or off-label use in hereditary angioedema, fibrocystic breast disease, immune thrombocytopenia and some other blood disorders [1][2][7].

In physique and hormone-optimisation communities, danazol is discussed mainly for one property: it binds sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and lowers its production, which raises the share of testosterone that circulates unbound. Forum users on T Nation describe it as a way to manage SHBG alongside testosterone replacement, with the aim of better energy, libido and training response, and through that more muscle and a leaner look [8][9][10]. These accounts are anecdotal; no published trial has tested danazol for physique or appearance.

It was synthesised in 1963 at Sterling Winthrop and approved by the US FDA in 1971 as the first drug specifically indicated for endometriosis; GnRH analogues have since largely replaced it for that purpose because they cause fewer masculinising effects [1]. Its androgenic effects include acne, excess hair growth and voice deepening that can persist after stopping [1][11].

angle.text: Community users take danazol, under a prescriber or otherwise, to lower SHBG and raise free testosterone while on testosterone therapy, aiming for better training and body composition. The SHBG effect is documented pharmacology, while the appearance outcome is a claim made in forum posts.

infobox: 3-10 hours after one dose; about 24-26 hours with chronic use

paras: The US label lists endometriosis amenable to hormonal management and prevention of hereditary angioedema attacks (cutaneous, abdominal and laryngeal) in men and women [11]. Off-label or regional uses described by Wikipedia include heavy menstrual bleeding, fibrocystic breast disease and breast pain, immune thrombocytopenic purpura, premenstrual syndrome and some features of lupus [1]. A 1982 review noted that approval for cystic breast disease followed endometriosis, and that researchers were using the drug to learn about several poorly understood diseases [22].
Capsules come in 50, 100 and 200 mg strengths, with daily amounts that vary by indication and are set by the prescriber [1].

subs.h: Use in physique and hormone communities
paras: Posts on T Nation describe danazol as an adjunct to testosterone replacement or hCG-based protocols, mentioned specifically for lowering SHBG [8][9][10]. One user reports that a physician prescribed a low amount alongside testosterone and hCG for that purpose [10]; another thread asks whether boron, said to lower SHBG, would interfere with an androgen already used to bind SHBG, naming danazol and Proviron [9]. Dosing and sourcing are not covered here.

In hereditary angioedema, the best-known result is a 1976 double-blind crossover study of nine patients: attacks followed 44 of 47 placebo courses but only one of 46 danazol courses, with C1 esterase inhibitor levels rising three- to fourfold and C4 about fifteenfold [3]. For endometriosis, a 1989 randomised comparison in 30 patients with laparoscopically confirmed implants found gestrinone and danazol each relieved disease in roughly 80-90 percent of cases over six months, with similar pregnancy rates and different side-effect profiles [12].

In breast cancer, Wikipedia reports response rates of about 15-20 percent [1]. For gynaecomastia, a 2023 review of the condition in boys states that clomiphene, danazol, letrozole and anastrozole have not been consistently useful in that age group, while tamoxifen has been tried successfully [13]. For physique outcomes there is no trial data.

A 2016 phase I/II NIH study in patients with telomere diseases reported effects on telomere length and blood counts, and Wikipedia notes it was stopped early after 12 of 27 patients met the primary efficacy endpoint [4][1]. Registered trials have examined danazol in telomere disease with low doses (NCT03312400, terminated, n=18), in Fanconi anaemia or dyskeratosis congenita (NCT01001598, terminated, n=5), in genetic bone marrow and lung disorders (NCT01441037, completed, n=27), and in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (NCT00953771, terminated, n=9) [5][6][14][15][16]. Several Chinese phase II registrations combine danazol with other drugs for steroid-resistant immune thrombocytopenia [17].

The MOMENTUM phase III trial used danazol as the active comparator for momelotinib in anaemic myelofibrosis patients previously treated with a JAK inhibitor, and it was published in 2023 in The Lancet and The Lancet Haematology [18][19]. A 2021 meta-analysis of 121 women with uterine arteriovenous malformation included danazol among medical treatments, with an overall 88 percent success rate across drug classes [20]. No studies were found of danazol for appearance or physique.

The label lists androgen-like effects such as weight gain, acne and seborrhoea, along with mild hirsutism, oedema, hair loss and voice changes (hoarseness, instability or deepening of pitch) that may persist after treatment ends; clitoral hypertrophy is rare. Menstrual disturbances and amenorrhoea are also listed [11]. Wikipedia adds unfavourable lipid changes, breast atrophy, hot flashes, raised liver enzymes, mood changes, and associations with benign liver tumours and, in endometriosis patients, ovarian cancer risk [1].

Danazol carries a boxed warning against use in pregnancy, because exposure in utero can masculinise a female fetus. The label recommends a sensitive early pregnancy test before therapy and non-hormonal contraception during it [11]. It is also contraindicated in liver disease, and long-term users are monitored with liver function tests [1]. A 1982 review described side effects as mild and reversible for most patients, while later sources emphasise that voice changes can persist [22][11].

Danazol suppresses the mid-cycle surge of LH and FSH, so it prevents ovulation without greatly lowering basal gonadotropins in premenopausal women. It inhibits several steroidogenic enzymes, including 17-alpha-hydroxylase, 17,20-lyase and 21-hydroxylase, and it markedly reduces adrenal, ovarian and testicular steroid output [1][2].

It binds the androgen receptor strongly, and the progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors to a moderate degree, while its oestrogen receptor affinity is poor. It also binds SHBG and corticosteroid-binding globulin, displacing hormones from them. Wikipedia reports that this raises free testosterone about threefold in women, and that danazol lowers SHBG production as well [1]. This SHBG action is the property discussed in physique communities. In men, danazol suppresses gonadotropins and lowers testosterone markedly, though spermatogenesis was reported to be unaffected even at high amounts [1].

Wikipedia describes danazol as roughly 200-fold less potent than testosterone in bioassays, with agonist and antagonist behaviour at the progesterone receptor depending on the assay and meaningful glucocorticoid receptor agonism that may explain immunosuppressive effects at higher exposures [1].

Oral bioavailability is low and saturable, and food, especially meals with more than 30 g of fat, raises absorption considerably. Peak levels occur at a median of about four hours. Half-life is 3-10 hours after one dose and about 24-26 hours with chronic use. CYP3A4 metabolises it into products including ethisterone and 2-hydroxymethylethisterone, which are excreted in urine and faeces [1]. Danazol is also a common model of a poorly water-soluble drug in dissolution and lipid-formulation research [21].

Sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) is a liver-made protein that binds testosterone and oestrogen; only about 1-4 percent of circulating testosterone is unbound, and the unbound fraction is the part that is biologically active [23]. Higher SHBG means less free testosterone, and lower SHBG means more; the ratio of testosterone to SHBG is used as the free androgen index [23]. Androgens and anabolic steroids lower SHBG, as do obesity, hypothyroidism and insulin resistance, while oestrogens, thyroid hormone and long-term calorie restriction raise it [23].

Danazol has high affinity for SHBG and displaces testosterone from it, and Wikipedia's SHBG article estimates that therapeutic levels would occupy or displace roughly 83-97 percent of its testosterone-binding sites [23]. Wikipedia's danazol article adds that in premenopausal women free testosterone roughly tripled, that the metabolite 2-hydroxymethylethisterone circulates at several times the parent drug's concentration and is about twice as potent at displacing testosterone from SHBG, and that danazol also reduces hepatic SHBG production [1]. In men, however, danazol markedly lowers gonadotropins and testosterone, so the net effect on free testosterone depends on the balance between these actions [1]. This is the mechanism that physique and testosterone-therapy forum users refer to when they discuss it [8][9][10].

A Sterling Winthrop team in Rensselaer, New York, including Helmut Neumann and Gordon Potts, synthesised danazol in 1963 under the code WIN-17757 [1]. The FDA approved it in 1971 as the first US drug specifically for endometriosis [1]. Cystic breast disease followed, and the 1976 hereditary angioedema study established a second major indication [3][6]. In the 2000s and 2010s, interest moved to haematology, including the 2016 telomere disease trial [4].

Gynaecological use shifted over time: GnRH analogues, which lack masculinising effects, largely replaced danazol for endometriosis [1]. Wikipedia also lists research uses in diabetic macular oedema (a phase III trial of low-dose danazol), breast cancer (response rates of about 15-20 percent) and telomere biology, including the 2016 NIH study in which 12 of 27 patients met the primary endpoint before it was stopped early [1][4].

For people who ask whether danazol changes how they look, the documented effects run in two directions. Its androgenic profile includes weight gain, acne, seborrhoea, hair loss, mild hirsutism and voice changes, and the label states that androgenic effects may not be reversible even after the drug is stopped [11]. Its antioestrogenic activity can reduce breast size in women [1]. The label also lists fluid retention and cramps among the commonly reported effects [11].

Forum users interested in body composition discuss the SHBG effect rather than direct muscle growth, with the aim of higher free testosterone, better training response and energy [8][9][10]. No published trial has measured muscle, fat or appearance outcomes with danazol.

The US label carries boxed warnings for pregnancy, thromboembolism (including sagittal sinus thrombosis and fatal strokes), peliosis hepatis and benign hepatic adenoma with long-term use, and benign intracranial hypertension [11]. Contraindications include undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding, markedly impaired liver, kidney or heart function, porphyria, androgen-dependent tumour and active thromboembolic disease [11]. Reversible liver-enzyme elevation is reported at higher amounts, and serious hepatic reactions are rare but listed [11]. The label also lists effects on the central nervous system (headache, mood changes, depression), skin reactions, and in men a modest reduction in spermatogenesis [11]. Danazol is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada and Australia [1].

Danazol is prescription-only in the US, the UK (POM), Canada and Australia (Schedule 4) and is marketed under many brand names including Danocrine, Danatrol and Danol, with one veterinary brand [1]. Within bodybuilding and testosterone-therapy circles it is mentioned as an SHBG-lowering agent, and forum users sometimes remark that clinics seldom bring it up [9]. Wikipedia classes it as an anabolic steroid, which is relevant to sport rules, though anti-doping status is not detailed here [1].

Within the testosterone-therapy conversation, SHBG management is discussed alongside other approaches, such as dietary boron, which one thread describes as lowering SHBG [24]. Danazol was marketed under the brand names Danocrine, Danatrol, Danoval and Winobanin among others, and the veterinary brand Dogalact exists [1]. Because Wikipedia classes danazol as an anabolic steroid, it falls into the group of agents that sport anti-doping rules concern, although its specific anti-doping status is not covered here [1].

lore.intro: On T Nation, danazol appears in threads about testosterone therapy, hCG and SHBG, usually as a prescribed or self-reported SHBG-lowering add-on [8][9][10].

claims.claim: Danazol lowers SHBG and raises free testosterone
claims.believers: Forum users say danazol "lowers SHBG really well" and discuss it as an add-on for people whose total testosterone looks adequate but whose free testosterone is low [8].
claims.experts: Pharmacology references confirm that danazol binds SHBG and reduces its production, raising free testosterone in women, although it also suppresses gonadotropins and lowers testosterone in men [1].

claims.claim: Danazol fixed symptoms that other approaches did not
claims.believers: One user reports that danazol was the only thing that worked for his low-libido, high-SHBG picture and says clinics rarely mention it [9].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested danazol for libido or energy in men on testosterone therapy; its approved uses are endometriosis and hereditary angioedema [11].

claims.claim: SHBG management is part of a complete hormone protocol
claims.believers: Users compare danazol with Proviron and boron as ways of managing SHBG and ask how they combine [10].
claims.experts: No human trial describes such combinations. Danazol's label lists androgenic side effects, liver monitoring and a pregnancy contraindication [11].

claims.claim: Raising free testosterone with danazol improves training and body composition.
claims.believers: Users on the forum link lower SHBG and higher free testosterone with better energy, libido and training response [8][10].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested danazol for physique or performance; in men it also suppresses gonadotropins and lowers testosterone [1].

claims.claim: Danazol is an anabolic steroid that builds muscle.
claims.believers: It is classed as an anabolic steroid, which leads some users to expect muscle-building effects [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports it is about 200-fold less potent than testosterone in bioassays, with weak androgenic activity; approved uses are endometriosis and hereditary angioedema [1][11].

claims.claim: Boron can replace danazol for lowering SHBG.
claims.believers: A forum thread titled around boron says its users find it helps, and another asks how it interacts with danazol and Proviron [24][9].
claims.experts: The danazol label and pharmacology literature do not address boron, and no trial compares the two [11].

claims.claim: Androgenic side effects fade after stopping.
claims.believers: Some users expect effects such as acne or hair changes to resolve.
claims.experts: The label says androgenic effects may not be reversible after stopping, and voice change can persist [11].

claims.claim: Danazol is a safe, mild add-on.
claims.believers: Users describe prescribed use under physician supervision as unremarkable [10].
claims.experts: The label carries boxed warnings for thromboembolism, liver lesions and intracranial hypertension, and is contraindicated in pregnancy [11].

card.summary: A prescription antigonadotropin steroid for endometriosis and angioedema; no evidence for appearance use.
card.note: Virilises female fetuses; masculinising side effects can be permanent.

quick.overview:
Danazol is an oral steroid prescribed for endometriosis, hereditary angioedema and some blood disorders. It has weak androgenic effects.

It has no studied role in appearance; mentions in muscle communities relate to its hormonal effects, not trials.
quick.mechanism: It suppresses LH and FSH, blocks several steroid-making enzymes and displaces hormones from SHBG, raising free testosterone. It also binds the androgen receptor.
quick.risks: Acne, hair growth, weight gain, lipid changes, liver enzyme elevation and permanent voice deepening are reported. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and prescription-only.
